editorial.headline: Natural-Medicine Retail: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity covers natural medicines for human use in shops, market stalls and street-vendor settings; it is nationally open to full foreign ownership but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
This is a retail activity for natural medicines intended for people, with a scope wider than the word herbal alone suggests. It includes jamu, standardised herbal medicines (OHT), phytopharmaceuticals and other natural medicines for human use. The materials may originate from plants, animals or minerals, while the goods may take the form of pills, capsules, powders or liquids. Health supplements and quasi-medicines also sit within the stated scope. In practical terms, the activity encompasses a natural-medicine shop as well as street vendors and market-stall traders dealing in these goods.

The recorded business scales span Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That range reflects a scope not confined to one retail setting: the same activity expressly includes fixed shops alongside informal market and street-trading formats. What unifies those settings is the retail sale of natural-medicine products for people, including the named traditional, herbal and phytopharmaceutical categories, rather than the size or appearance of the selling venue.

At the national level, PMA is TERBUKA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. A fully foreign-owned PMA position is therefore available at the national level for this activity; the foreign stake is not capped below full ownership. The stated national basis is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. This distinction deserves careful reading: national openness establishes the ownership ceiling for the activity, but it does not by itself settle whether PMA registration is available in every location.

In Bali, the conclusion is direct: a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA. The record marks it as blocked because, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope. Bali’s moratorium, effective May 13, 2026, blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the island on a permanent basis. The national 100% ceiling remains the national position, but it does not overcome this Bali-specific PMA block.
